title: The Geonim
hook: heads of the Babylonian academies answer questions from Jews across the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Babylonian Talmud: a first page that asks where the teacher is standing, and Rav Ashi and Ravina as the end. Your line was the talmud sealed. Did you ask where a rule comes from? Day nine hundred eleven.

A community in Kairouan, in North Africa, has a question it can't settle. Not about a holiday or a meal. A history question: how was the Mishnah written? And the Talmud, how did it come together? Who did what, and in what order? So Rabbi Jacob ben Nissim, a teacher there, writes a letter and send it a very long way east, to the head of the academy at Pumbedita. And an answer comes back. The answer is long, careful, and so useful that people are still reading it. We're starting a new stretch of the story today: Babylon, the Islamic world, and the first Ashkenazim.
screen: `A QUESTION IN KAIROUAN.` → `HOW WAS THE MISHNAH WRITTEN?` → `A LETTER EAST TO PUMBEDITA.`

segments.voice: After the Talmud was sealed, the academies of Sura and Pumbedita went on. Their heads came to carry a title: Gaon, and in the plural, Geonim. The title is usually explained as short for the head of the academy that is the pride of Jacob. That phrase comes from a psalm, which in the 1917 Jewish translation reads "The pride of Jacob whom He loveth." In everyday Hebrew, gaon came to mean a genius. But here it is a job title, and the job was to teach, and to answer. Jewish communities were spread across a huge distance. The Talmud was the shared text, but it is long and hard, and real life keeps producing cases it never quite covered. So letters traveled to the Geonim. The Geonim read the question, studied it, and wrote back. The letter from Kairouan reached Rav Sherira Gaon, head of Pumbedita. His reply, known as the Letter of Rav Sherira Gaon, walks through how the Mishnah and the Talmud took shape, teacher by teacher. Here is the picture to hold. A text sealed in one place, and a web of letters spreading it to many others. Letters across the world. A question written in one city, an answer written in another, and the conversation of the academies reaching people who had never seen them.
screen: `GAON: HEAD OF THE ACADEMY.` · `THE PRIDE OF JACOB.` · `THE LETTER OF RAV SHERIRA GAON.` · then, large: `LETTERS ACROSS THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to write down one question. Sit, and let the first breaths settle. Then let a real question come to mind, not a quiz question, a question you actually carry. About your tradition, your family's story, a text you never understood, a choice in front of you. Don't answer it. Just find the words for it, the way the people of Kairouan found theirs. Make it clear enough that someone far away could understand it. After the bell, write it down somewhere you'll see it again. If you pray, you can bring that question to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Gaon. The title of the heads of the Babylonian academies, the Geonim, who answered questions sent from far away. Today's word.
Your line: letters across the world. Today, send one real message to someone far away, a question or a thank you, written with care. Day nine hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Jews today still turn to the Geonim's surviving letters and rulings as early witnesses to how the Talmud was read, and historians study the Letter of Rav Sherira Gaon for its account of the Mishnah and Talmud.

original.note: Hebrew: pride or excellence; the title of the heads of the Babylonian academies.

trapdoor: what you thought: gaon means a genius.
what it means: the title of the heads of Sura and Pumbedita, who answered questions by letter.
what a scholar hears: the title is usually explained as short for head of the academy of the pride of Jacob, a phrase from Psalm 47.

notes: New part begins: 'Babylon, the Islamic world, and the first Ashkenazim'; the hook names it.

Iggeret Rav Sherira Gaon: written in answer to questions from Kairouan (sent by Rabbi Jacob ben Nissim) on how the Mishnah and Talmud were written. Confirm the framing and that Sherira headed Pumbedita.
'Gaon' explained as short for 'Rosh Yeshivat Ge'on Ya'akov' (Psalm 47:5 Hebrew); hedged as 'usually explained'. Confirm.
'Letters carried by merchants and travelers along trade routes' is general; confirm.
'People are still reading it' and howItsDone describe ongoing study of Sherira's letter; confirm.
